passages.happening:
God tells Moses to have Israel “turn back and encamp before Pi-hahiroth, between Migdol and the sea” (verse 2). “For Pharaoh will say of the Israelites, ‘They are wandering the land in confusion; the wilderness has boxed them in.’ And I will harden Pharaoh’s heart so that he will pursue them. But I will gain honor by means of Pharaoh and all his army, and the Egyptians will know that I am the LORD” (verses 3-4).

When the king hears that the people have fled, “Pharaoh and his officials changed their minds about them and said, ‘What have we done? We have released Israel from serving us’” (verse 5). He takes “600 of the best chariots, and all the other chariots of Egypt” (verse 7), and overtakes Israel camped by the sea (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
This chapter tells the event the rest of the Bible remembers as the great act of salvation in the Old Testament. The plagues broke Pharaoh's will. The sea breaks his power.

God leads Israel into what looks like a trap, with the sea in front. It is on purpose. Pharaoh will think they are lost and come after them.

The place names, Pi-hahiroth, Migdol and Baal-zephon, have not been securely located. Migdol means tower or fort, a common name for Egyptian border posts. Baal-zephon is named after a Canaanite god, Baal of the north, whose worship is known from Egypt's eastern Delta.

Pharaoh's regret is telling: ‘We have released Israel from serving us.’ What he misses is not his firstborn. It is his workforce.

The chariot was the elite weapon of Egypt in this period. Egyptian carvings show light two-wheeled chariots carrying a driver and a fighter, usually an archer. They could run down people on foot in open country. Six hundred of the best, and all the rest, against a people with no army.

And again, ‘I will harden Pharaoh's heart’. The chapter notes on Exodus 4 and 9 set out how Christians read this.
passages.later:
Psalm 106 remembers the God who acted here “for the sake of His name, to make His power known” (Psalm 106:8).

Paul quotes God's word to Pharaoh, that God raised him up “that I might display My power in you, and that My name might be proclaimed in all the earth” (Romans 9:17).
passages.asks: Pharaoh missed his slaves more than he grieved his losses. Ask what you hold on to so tightly that you would chase it into danger. And ask what it would mean to let it go.

passages.happening:
“As Pharaoh approached, the Israelites looked up and saw the Egyptians marching after them, and they were terrified and cried out to the LORD” (verse 10).

They say to Moses, “Was it because there were no graves in Egypt that you brought us into the wilderness to die?” (verse 11). “For it would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in the wilderness” (verse 12).

“But Moses told the people, ‘Do not be afraid. Stand firm and you will see the LORD’s salvation, which He will accomplish for you today; for the Egyptians you see today, you will never see again. The LORD will fight for you; you need only to be still’” (verses 13-14).
passages.hearers:
Israel's fear is real. Runaway slaves are facing professional soldiers, with the sea at their backs.

‘No graves in Egypt?’ is bitter sarcasm, because Egypt was famous for its tombs. They would rather go back to slavery than die free. It is a hard thing to admit, and the Bible admits it. People who have known slavery for a long time can find freedom frightening.

Moses' answer is one of the great sentences of the Bible. ‘Do not be afraid. Stand firm.’ And then: ‘The LORD will fight for you.’ Israel does not have to win this battle. They have to watch God win it.

Notice the word ‘see’. Israel sees the Egyptians and is afraid. Moses says they will see the LORD's salvation, and never see these Egyptians again. The chapter moves their fear, step by step, from the enemy to God.
passages.later:
King Jehoshaphat's people hear the same promise in a later crisis: “You need not fight this battle. Take up your positions, stand firm, and see the salvation of the LORD on your behalf” (2 Chronicles 20:17).

The psalm says, “Be still and know that I am God” (Psalm 46:10).
passages.asks: The people would have gone back to slavery rather than face the unknown. Ask whether there is an old slavery you are tempted to go back to because it feels safer than freedom. And ask what it would mean, in your situation, to stand firm and let God fight for you.

passages.happening:
“Then the LORD said to Moses, ‘Why are you crying out to Me? Tell the Israelites to go forward. And as for you, lift up your staff and stretch out your hand over the sea and divide it, so that the Israelites can go through the sea on dry ground’” (verses 15-16).

“And the angel of God, who had gone before the camp of Israel, withdrew and went behind them. The pillar of cloud also moved from before them and stood behind them” (verse 19). It came between the two camps. “The cloud was there in the darkness, but it lit up the night. So all night long neither camp went near the other” (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
‘Why are you crying out to me?’ There is a time to pray and a time to move. Now it is time to go forward.

The pillar that led them now moves behind them. It stands between Israel and the army. To Egypt it is darkness; to Israel it lights up the night. The God who went ahead of them now guards them from behind.

An ancient reader would hear more than a battle here. Pharaoh was seen as a god on earth, the keeper of order against chaos. Egyptian royal art often shows him in his chariot trampling foreign enemies. And across the ancient world the sea was a picture of chaos; in Canaanite stories the god Baal fought the sea god. Here the LORD commands the sea like a servant, beside a place named for Baal, and uses it against the chariots of the god-king. ‘I will gain honor by means of Pharaoh’ is a claim about who truly rules.
passages.later: The prophets sing of the God who “makes a way in the sea and a path through the surging waters” (Isaiah 43:16), and ask, “Was it not You who dried up the sea, the waters of the great deep, who made a road in the depths of the sea for the redeemed to cross over?” (Isaiah 51:10).
passages.asks: God said, ‘Why are you crying out to Me?’ and ‘go forward’. Ask whether there is a step you have been praying about that God has already told you to take. And ask what it would mean to trust that he is guarding you from behind as well as leading you ahead.

passages.t: Through the sea on dry ground
passages.happening:
“Then Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and all that night the LORD drove back the sea with a strong east wind that turned it into dry land. So the waters were divided, and the Israelites went through the sea on dry ground, with walls of water on their right and on their left” (verses 21-22).

The Egyptians follow them into the sea (verse 23). “At morning watch, however, the LORD looked down on the army of the Egyptians from the pillar of fire and cloud, and He threw their camp into confusion. He caused their chariot wheels to wobble, so that they had difficulty driving” (verses 24-25). “‘Let us flee from the Israelites,’ said the Egyptians, ‘for the LORD is fighting for them against Egypt!’” (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
The text names a means: ‘a strong east wind’ that blew ‘all that night’. It also says the waters stood like walls on either side. The Bible does not set God's action against the wind. It says God used it.

The night was divided into watches, and the ‘morning watch’ was the last, before dawn. Soldiers expected to attack at first light. Instead the army is caught on the sea bed in the dark, with wheels that will not run true. The Egyptians themselves say what is happening: ‘the LORD is fighting for them’.
passages.later:
Joshua compares the crossing of the Jordan with this one: “just as He did to the Red Sea, which He dried up before us until we had crossed over” (Joshua 4:23).

The psalm says, “Your path led through the sea, Your way through the mighty waters, but Your footprints were not to be found. You led Your people like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron” (Psalm 77:19-20).

Paul says Israel's ancestors “were all baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Corinthians 10:2), treating the passage through the water, under God's presence, as a picture of baptism: passing from slavery into a new life. Hebrews lists it as faith: “By faith the people passed through the Red Sea as on dry land” (Hebrews 11:29).
passages.hard:
Where did Israel cross, and what happened at the sea?

The place is not known. The Hebrew name, yam suph, means sea of reeds. The Bible uses it for the Gulf of Suez and for the Gulf of Aqaba (1 Kings 9:26), and perhaps also for marshy lakes nearer Egypt. Places proposed for the crossing include the Gulf of Suez, the Bitter Lakes or Lake Timsah along the line of the modern Suez Canal, a lagoon on the Mediterranean coast, and the Gulf of Aqaba. The place names in verse 2 have not been securely located, so the question stays open. No map with these notes draws a crossing point for that reason.

How it happened is read in more than one way. Some accept the account as it stands, a direct act of God. Others look for natural processes God used, since the text itself names an east wind blowing all night. Others again regard the story as Israel's later, poetic memory of how it began.

Christians who hold Scripture as God's word take more than one view of the place and the means, and these notes take no side. On every reading, the chapter's claim is that the LORD saved Israel.
passages.asks: God made a way where there was none. Ask what sea is in front of you, with no road across. And ask whether you can trust the God who makes paths through the waters, even when his footprints cannot be seen.

passages.happening:
God tells Moses to stretch out his hand again, “so that the waters may flow back over the Egyptians and their chariots and horsemen” (verse 26). He does, “and at daybreak the sea returned to its normal state. As the Egyptians were retreating, the LORD swept them into the sea” (verse 27). “Not one of them survived” (verse 28).

“But the Israelites had walked through the sea on dry ground, with walls of water on their right and on their left” (verse 29). “That day the LORD saved Israel from the hand of the Egyptians, and Israel saw the Egyptians dead on the shore” (verse 30).

“When Israel saw the great power that the LORD had exercised over the Egyptians, the people feared the LORD and believed in Him and in His servant Moses” (verse 31).
passages.hearers:
The sentence ‘on dry ground, with walls of water on their right and on their left’ comes twice, in verses 22 and 29. It frames the crossing like two walls.

The chapter ends where it began, with the word ‘fear’. In verse 10 Israel feared the Egyptians. Now they fear the LORD, and believe him. That is the whole movement of the chapter: from fear of the enemy to reverent trust in God.

The army is gone. ‘Not one of them survived.’ The text does not hide the deaths. Israel ‘saw the Egyptians dead on the shore’.
passages.later:
Israel sang of it at once: “I will sing to the LORD, for He is highly exalted. The horse and rider He has thrown into the sea” (Exodus 15:1). Psalm 106 says, “The waters covered their foes; not one of them remained. Then they believed His promises and sang His praise” (Psalm 106:11-12).

Yet the Bible also warns against delight in an enemy's fall: “Do not gloat when your enemy falls, and do not let your heart rejoice when he stumbles” (Proverbs 24:17). And God asks through Ezekiel, “Do I take any pleasure in the death of the wicked?” (Ezekiel 18:23).
passages.hard:
How should we think about the Egyptian soldiers who drowned? The drowning of the army is harder to feel than to explain. The text presents it as judgment on a power that had enslaved Israel and ordered the killing of its infant sons, and as the last act of a long contest in which Pharaoh was warned again and again. The soldiers are not judged one by one; they belong to the power that is destroyed.

Later Jewish tradition tells a well-known story in which God rebukes the angels for wanting to sing while his creatures drown. And Ezekiel 18:23 insists that God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked. The Bible celebrates the rescue without asking anyone to take pleasure in death. Many of those soldiers had families who never saw them again.

The hardening of Pharaoh's heart comes up once more in this chapter (verses 4, 8 and 17). Christians in the Reformed tradition read it as God's sovereign purpose working through Pharaoh's real choices; many in the Arminian tradition, and some Jewish readers, stress that Pharaoh hardened himself first and that God's hardening confirmed the road he chose. Both agree that Pharaoh is never pictured as a man who wanted to do right and was stopped. Faithful readers differ, and these notes take no side.
passages.asks: Israel's fear moved from the enemy to God. Ask what you fear most right now, and whether it has more hold on you than God does. And ask whether you can thank God for rescue without hating those who were on the other side.
